DOCUMENT:
Menu Pricing Review: Spring 2026
The Copper Kettle, prepared by the General Manager for the owners, March 2026

1. Purpose
This paper reviews main-course pricing and menu mix and proposes changes to take effect with the spring menu on 1 April 2026. Our overall gross margin on food, across all courses, has slipped from 70% to 67% over the past year as ingredient costs have risen faster than our prices, and we last changed main-course prices in September 2024.

2. Trading pattern
The Copper Kettle is a 64-cover restaurant open for lunch and dinner from Wednesday to Sunday. We serve an average of 1,050 main courses a week, with Friday and Saturday dinner accounting for just under half. Our customers are mainly local, with a strong repeat base: our booking system shows that around 60% of bookings come from guests who have dined with us in the past six months.

Table 1. Main courses, average weekly sales (January-February 2026)
Dish | Menu price | Food cost per plate | Gross margin | Plates per week
Fish and chips | £16.50 | £5.10 | 69% | 310
Beef burger | £15.00 | £4.20 | 72% | 260
Chicken curry | £14.50 | £3.60 | 75% | 180
Sirloin steak | £26.00 | £10.40 | 60% | 120
Mushroom risotto | £14.00 | £2.80 | 80% | 90
Other mains (specials) | various | various | 64% | 90

3. Competitor prices
We checked menus at the five restaurants we regard as our closest competitors. Their fish and chips ranges from £16.95 to £19.00, burgers from £15.50 to £17.50 and sirloin steak from £27.00 to £32.00. Our prices for these three dishes are the lowest in the group.

4. Supplier costs
Our meat supplier has given notice that beef prices will rise by 12% from 1 April 2026, reflecting national cattle prices. Other supplier prices are expected to be broadly stable over the spring. Fish prices have been volatile but are currently close to their 2025 average.

5. Proposals
5.1 Price increases. Raise fish and chips to £17.50, the beef burger to £16.00 and the sirloin steak to £28.00. All three would remain below the midpoint of the competitor range for that dish.

5.2 Remove the mushroom risotto. Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place. We propose replacing it with a seasonal vegetarian special at the same price.

5.3 Projected effect. If volumes hold, the price increases add £1.00 per plate on 310 fish and chips, £1.00 on 260 burgers and £2.00 on 120 steaks, a total of £810 a week in additional gross profit, or £42,120 a year. Because our prices remain competitive and our customer base is loyal, we expect volumes to hold. The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target.

6. Communication
Menus will be reprinted for 1 April. Staff will be briefed on the changes, and we will not draw attention to the increases on the menu. We will monitor plates sold per dish weekly for the first eight weeks against the January to February baseline.

7. Risks
Some regular guests may notice the increases. However, the last price change in 2024 had no visible effect on bookings, and the new prices remain competitive. Weekday lunch trade is more price-sensitive than dinner, but it represents a small share of main-course sales.

8. Recommendation
We recommend that the owners approve the three price increases and the replacement of the mushroom risotto from 1 April 2026. Together these changes add about £42,000 a year in gross profit, improve our margin and keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [misread_evidence] at: "Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place." -- Table 1 shows mushroom risotto has the highest gross margin on the menu (80%); the weakest is sirloin steak (60%). Lowest sales is correct (90 plates, tied with specials), but the margin claim misreads the table.
2. [missing_consideration] at: "The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target." -- The projection uses current food costs, but section 4 states beef prices rise 12% from 1 April, the same date as the new prices. Burgers and steaks (380 plates a week) would see higher food costs (e.g. about £1.25 more per steak), eroding much of the projected gain; the margin and profit projections never account for it.
3. [inconsistency] at: "keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week" -- Section 2 says the restaurant is open Wednesday to Sunday, i.e. five days a week; the recommendation refers to six trading days.

REVIEW:
# Review: Menu Pricing Review, Spring 2026 (The Copper Kettle)

## Summary of the proposal

The paper proposes three main-course price rises from 1 April: fish and chips £16.50 → £17.50, burger £15.00 → £16.00, sirloin £26.00 → £28.00. It also proposes replacing the mushroom risotto with a seasonal vegetarian special. It projects £810 a week (£42,120 a year) of extra gross profit and a main-course margin of about 71%. Its stated goal is to recover an overall food margin that has fallen from 70% to 67%.

Some of the paper's claims check out:
- The table's margins are correct.
- £810 × 52 is £42,120.
- Each new price is below the midpoint of the competitor range (£17.98, £16.50 and £29.50).

But the projection leaves out a cost change the paper itself reports. The risotto decision rests on a misreading of the paper's own table. Once both are corrected, the package as written *lowers* main-course margin rather than raising it to 71%.

## 1. The 12% beef increase is left out of the projection

Section 4 says beef rises 12% from 1 April, the same day the new prices start. Section 5.3 ignores it.

| Dish | Food cost now | From 1 April | Extra cost per plate | Price rise | Net gain per plate | Plates/wk | Net £/wk |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Fish and chips | £5.10 | £5.10 | — | £1.00 | £1.00 | 310 | £310 |
| Beef burger | £4.20 | £4.70 | £0.50 | £1.00 | £0.50 | 260 | £129 |
| Sirloin steak | £10.40 | £11.65 | £1.25 | £2.00 | £0.75 | 120 | £90 |
| **Total** | | | | | | | **£529** |

Compared with today, the gain is about **£529 a week (£27,500 a year)**, not £810.

The £810 is right in one narrow sense: it is the gain compared with keeping current prices *after* beef rises. But the paper presents it as an improvement on today and uses it to claim a 71% margin. On that basis it is overstated by about a third. Two-fifths of the steak increase and half the burger increase only cover the higher beef cost.

The steak margin actually **falls**, from 60% to about 58%. The burger falls from 72% to about 71%.

## 2. The risotto has the *highest* margin on the menu, not the weakest

Section 5.2 and the author's description both say risotto "has the weakest margin on the menu." Table 1 shows the opposite.

| | Margin | Gross profit per plate |
|---|---|---|
| Mushroom risotto | **80% (highest)** | £11.20 |
| Sirloin steak | 60% (lowest) | £15.60 |
| Other specials | 64% | — |

Risotto is tied with specials for the lowest sales (90 a week), so that part of the claim is right. But it earns £11.20 a plate, more than the burger or the curry, and about £1,000 a week in total.

The replacement is a special "at the same price." At the 64% margin specials currently make, it would earn about £8.96 a plate. That is **about £200 a week (£10,500 a year) less** at the same volume.

The swap only breaks even if the new special's food cost is £2.80 or less. Unless it is costed to that level, keep the risotto. If the problem is low sales, re-promoting it is cheaper than replacing it.

It may also be the only vegetarian main besides whatever special is running. Losing it risks group bookings where one diner is vegetarian.

## 3. The margin claim reverses once both corrections are made

Using the five dishes with known prices (specials excluded because their prices aren't given):

| Scenario | Main-course margin |
|---|---|
| Today | 69.9% |
| Price rises only, ignoring beef (the paper's basis) | 71.3% |
| Price rises with beef increase | 69.7% |
| Price rises, beef increase and risotto swap at 64% | **68.5%** |

As written, the package moves the main-course margin from about 70% to about 68.5%.

There is a second point here. Mains are already at about 70%, so they are not where the overall food margin fell to 67%. The erosion is in starters, desserts, sides or specials, and this paper doesn't look at any of them. Price rises on mains can't restore the overall target if the problem is elsewhere.

## 4. VAT

UK menu prices normally include 20% VAT, and the table appears to calculate margins on VAT-inclusive prices. If so:
- Every margin is overstated. Fish and chips, for example, is about 63% on its net price, not 69%.
- Each £1 rise brings in only about £0.83 of revenue.

On a net-of-VAT basis, the price rises after the beef increase add about £394 a week. With the risotto swap included, the total is about **£190 a week (about £10,000 a year)**, a quarter of the £42,000 headline.

Please confirm how the margins in Table 1 are calculated and state it in the paper.

## 5. Volume and demand

The whole projection rests on "if volumes hold." The supporting evidence is weaker than the paper suggests.

- **"We remain the value option."** Today these are the lowest prices in the group. After the rises, all three dishes are above the cheapest competitor (£16.95, £15.50 and £27.00). Below the midpoint is accurate. Cheapest no longer is.
- **The 60% repeat-booking figure.** Loyal regulars are often the people most likely to *notice* a price rise. The figure also covers bookings, not covers, and excludes walk-ins.
- **"No visible effect" in 2024.** This refers to bookings. Bookings could stay level while guests switch to cheaper dishes or order fewer extras.
- **Substitution.** Guests may switch from burger or steak to the unchanged curry, which has a lower cash margin.
- **Weekday lunch is a "small share."** This isn't supported. Friday and Saturday dinner make up just under half of mains, and the paper doesn't say how the other half divides between lunch and dinner.

How much volume can be lost before each rise stops paying for itself (comparing with current prices after the beef increase)?
- fish and chips: about 8%
- burger: about 9%
- steak: about 12%

Those are plausible but not trivial losses.

## 6. Monitoring

- **The baseline is seasonal.** Comparing April–May volumes against January–February will mix up price effects with normal spring trade.
- **A better comparison:** the same weeks last year, or the dishes whose prices aren't changing. The curry is an obvious internal control.
- **No decision rule.** Set a threshold in advance, for example "if fish and chips falls more than 8% relative to the curry over four weeks, review." Otherwise eight weeks of data won't lead to any decision.

## 7. Smaller points

- **Trading days.** The recommendation says "six trading days a week." Section 2 says Wednesday to Sunday, which is five.
- **Annualising.** £42,120 is two months of January–February volume multiplied by 52, with no adjustment for seasonality or closures.
- **Fish prices.** Fish is described as volatile, and fish and chips is the biggest seller. That is a margin risk the paper doesn't mention.
- **Communication.** Not drawing attention to the increases is reasonable. But staff should be ready to explain the beef cost if regulars ask.

## Suggested revisions

1. Restate the projection including the beef increase, and say whether figures are gross or net of VAT. The honest figure is about £27,500 a year gross of VAT, or about £20,500 net, before the risotto change.
2. Drop the risotto removal, or make it conditional on a special costed at £2.80 or less.
3. Withdraw the 71% margin claim, and extend the review to starters, desserts and specials, where the fall to 67% probably happened.
4. Describe the new prices as "below the competitor midpoint," not "the value option."
5. Monitor against last year's same weeks and the curry, with volume thresholds set in advance.
6. Correct "six trading days" to five.

The price rises themselves are defensible: costs have risen, there has been no change since 2024, and the new prices are still below the competitor midpoint. The case for them is "this roughly covers the beef increase and adds a modest margin," not "£42,000 a year and 71%." The risotto change should not go ahead as written.
